prompt:
36-year-old man diagnosed with HIV two weeks ago (CD4 42 cells/uL, viral load 280,000 copies/mL), not yet on antiretroviral therapy, started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis at diagnosis. He now reports ten days of worsening headache, nausea, low-grade fevers, and intermittent blurred vision. He is alert and oriented with mild neck stiffness and no focal neurologic deficits. Temperature 38.1 C, BP 128/80. His primary care physician plans to start antiretroviral therapy in clinic today and prescribe sumatriptan for the headaches. Is that the right plan?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Suspect cryptococcal meningitis and arrange urgent same-day evaluation.
Perform a lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement.
Treat induction with liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, or an equivalent guideline regimen.
Perform therapeutic lumbar punctures to reduce elevated opening pressure (25 cm H2O or more).
Defer antiretroviral therapy until about four to six weeks after starting antifungal therapy.
Check serum cryptococcal antigen.
Send CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, bacterial and fungal cultures, and cryptococcal antigen.
Obtain head CT or MRI before lumbar puncture given advanced immunosuppression.
Monitor potassium, magnesium, and creatinine and give pre-hydration with amphotericin B.
Continue trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis.
Arrange an ophthalmologic exam for the visual symptoms, including assessment for papilledema.
Follow induction with fluconazole consolidation and then maintenance therapy.
Obtain infectious diseases consultation.
Admit to the hospital.
Assess mental status serially and repeat lumbar puncture for recurrent headache or signs of raised pressure.
Send CSF for additional pathogens such as mycobacteria, syphilis, and herpesviruses as indicated.
Obtain blood cultures, including fungal cultures.
Monitor flucytosine levels and CBC.
Screen for other opportunistic infections and coinfections, including tuberculosis, toxoplasma IgG, syphilis, and hepatitis B.
Review fluconazole interactions when selecting antiretroviral therapy.
Monitor for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after antiretroviral therapy starts.
Repeat lumbar puncture at about two weeks to document CSF sterilization.
Provide adherence counseling and linkage to HIV care.
Provide antiemetics and non-NSAID analgesia.
Start antiretroviral therapy today.
Discharge with sumatriptan for presumed migraine.
Treat with an echinocandin such as caspofungin.
Use fluconazole monotherapy for induction when amphotericin B is available.
Use acetazolamide to lower intracranial pressure.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone.
Skip the opening pressure measurement.
Stop trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Use a negative India ink stain alone to exclude cryptococcal infection.
Delay antifungal therapy until the CSF culture grows Cryptococcus.
Treat empirically for bacterial meningitis only.
Skip lumbar puncture once serum cryptococcal antigen is positive.
Give amphotericin B deoxycholate without hydration or electrolyte monitoring.
Give mannitol for elevated intracranial pressure.
Place a ventriculoperitoneal shunt as first-line pressure management.
Start empiric toxoplasmosis therapy without neuroimaging.
